Apr 18Breakthrough Prize: Frank Merle ($3M) for nonlinear evolution equationsRelevant: PDE behavior, singularity formation — adjacent to Navier-Stokes.

10. The Map Is Not the Territory

This scan found ~$15M in open bounties across ~130 problems in the P/NP/complexity/compression landscape. The largest concentrations are:

  • $6M in Clay Millennium Prizes (5 open + 1 active)
  • $2M in ARC-AGI prizes (annual, 2026)
  • $1M+ in Beal, IUT disproof, Proximity Prize
  • €500K in Hutter Prize (incremental)
  • $3M/yr in Breakthrough Prizes (nomination-based)

The ecoPrimals work intersects most directly with:

  1. P vs NP (baseCamp 42 — we made the statement, Clay wants the proof)
  2. Hutter Prize (epitope sort is a compression algorithm — the bridge is buildable)
  3. ARC-AGI (accept-and-generate is the methodology — the score would validate the framework)
  4. Riemann / Yang-Mills (baseCamp 50 — π as dimensional cost, if formalized)

But the bounty is not the point. The bounty is the by-product. The point is: can we test the hypothesis? The next test is not the $1M proof. The next test is T6 — can elastic collisions in a billiard box produce digits of π in a way that confirms π is a dimensional cost, not just a geometric ratio?

The environment is catalogued. The terrain is mapped. The organism knows where it is.

Now move.

baseCamp 51 — Environmental scan by eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

The map is not the territory, but a good map tells you where to step next.

entry.title: baseCamp 52 — GoG + Manim: Full Life via the Dimensional Equation
entry.content:
Architectural hypothesis. October 10, 2026.

Abstract

petalTongue contains two visualization engines that together provide every capability needed for “full life” — a living, breathing, mathematically grounded visual experience of the organism:

  1. GoG — Grammar of Graphics (grammar.rs): data binding → variable mapping → scale transformation → geometry selection → coordinate system → faceting → aesthetic rendering → scene graph. This is Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics (1999) implemented as a Rust scene compiler.

  2. Equation Compiler (equation.rs): LaTeX-like mathematical notation → scene primitives. Fractions, superscripts, subscripts, Greek letters, operators, integrals. Manim-style math rendering without external LaTeX dependency.

Each engine is individually functional. Neither alone produces full life. GoG renders data without mathematical truth. The equation compiler renders truth without living data. Together — GoG × Equation × Animation × Physics — they produce what the HUD is trying to be: a living dashboard where the organism’s vital signs are both measured (GoG) and understood (equations), animated (flow particles, pulses), and physically simulated (n-body, collisions).

The missing ingredient: the dimensional equation from baseCamp 50.

C(n) ∝ π^(n/2)

This cost function should shape the visualization itself — elements with more dimensions cost more visual weight, more attention, more rendering time. And the layout should evolve via epitope sort — not fixed grids, but behavioral clustering where panels that belong together drift together.

1. What Exists

1.1 Grammar of Graphics Engine

petal-tongue-scene/src/grammar.rs

The GoG engine has the full Wilkinson specification:

LayerImplementationStatus
Datadata_source: String — binds to live data feeds✓
VariablesVariableBinding { name, field, role } — x, y, z, color, size, shape, label, detail✓
ScalesScaleType — Linear, Log, Temporal, Categorical, Ordinal, Sqrt✓
GeometryGeometryType — Point, Line, Bar, Area, Ribbon, Tile, Arc, ErrorBar, Mesh3D, Sphere, Cylinder, Text✓
CoordinatesCoordinateSystem — Cartesian, Polar, Geographic, Perspective3D✓
FacetsFacetLayout — Wrap(columns), Grid(rows, cols)✓
AestheticsFill, Stroke, Size, Alpha, Shape, Label✓

This is the structural engine. It takes data and produces shapes. The HUD panels that show bar charts, donut charts, scatter plots — those are GoG output.

1.2 Equation Compiler (Manim Engine)

petal-tongue-scene/src/equation.rs

The equation compiler converts LaTeX-like strings into scene primitives:

FeatureSyntaxOutput
Fractions\frac{a}{b}Text + Line (fraction bar)
Superscriptsx^{2}, x^2Raised text
Subscriptsx_{i}, x_iLowered text
Greek\alpha, \pi, \sigmaUnicode characters
Operators\sum, \prod, \int, \sqrtOperator glyphs
Symbols\infty, \pm, \cdot, \leq, \neqSymbol characters

This is the mathematical truth engine. It renders equations as visual objects. When the HUD shows H(data|epitope) < H(data|alphabet) < H(data), this engine renders it.

1.3 Math Module

petal-tongue-scene/src/math/
├── axes.rs          — Coordinate axes with ticks, labels, ranges
├── curves.rs        — FunctionPlot (y=f(x)), ParametricCurve ((x(t), y(t)))
└── vector_field.rs  — VectorField: F(x,y) → (dx, dy) as arrow grids

This bridges GoG and equations. It can plot functions, trace parametric curves, and render vector fields — the visual language of physics.

1.4 Physics Engine

petal-tongue-scene/src/physics.rs

N-body simulation with collision shapes (Sphere, Box), gravity, Euler integration. This is where baseCamp 50 lives visually — three bodies orbiting, the dimensional cost visible as trajectory chaos.

1.5 Animation Engine

petal-tongue-animation/
├── flower.rs         — Flower opening (awakening experience)
├── visual_flower.rs  — High-quality visual flower rendering
└── lib.rs            — FlowParticle, NodePulse, BandwidthGlow

This is the “life” — particles flowing along edges, nodes pulsing with activity, flowers opening as the organism awakens.

1.6 Multi-Modal Output

petal-tongue-scene/src/modality/
├── svg.rs            — SVG rendering (production)
├── webgl.rs          — WebGL rendering (GPU accelerated)
├── terminal.rs       — Terminal/TUI rendering
├── audio.rs          — Audio sonification
├── braille/          — Braille rendering (accessibility)
├── haptic.rs         — Haptic feedback
└── description.rs    — Natural language description

Every visualization can be rendered through any of 7 modalities. This is already more than Manim (Python, video only) and ggplot (R, static image only).

2. What’s Missing: The Dimensional Equation

2.1 The Cost Function

baseCamp 50 proposes:

C(n) ∝ π^(n/2)

The cost of observing n dimensions scales as π raised to half the dimension count. In visualization terms: a 1D line costs π^(0.5) ≈ 1.77 units of attention. A 2D plot costs π ≈ 3.14. A 3D mesh costs π^(1.5) ≈ 5.57. A 4D projection costs π² ≈ 9.87.

This is not an arbitrary scaling law. If baseCamp 50 is correct, this is the physical cost of angular observation — and it should appear naturally in any system that renders high-dimensional data as visual experience.

2.2 How It Shapes Visualization

Currently, the HUD renders all panels at equal visual weight — 3×3 grid, equal size, equal prominence. This is democratically wrong. Some panels contain more dimensions of information than others:

HUD PanelData DimensionsC(n) ∝ π^(n/2)Visual Weight
Live Signal1 (RPS over time)π^(0.5) ≈ 1.77Low
Epitope Summary2 (epitope × count)π ≈ 3.14Medium
Entity Population2 (entity × volume)π ≈ 3.14Medium
Fleet Honesty1 (ratio)π^(0.5) ≈ 1.77Low
Bingo Cube3 (attention × curiosity × interaction)π^(1.5) ≈ 5.57High
Collision Detection2 (pattern × frequency)π ≈ 3.14Medium
ASN Infrastructure2 (ASN × request count)π ≈ 3.14Medium

The Bingo Cube panel should be visually larger than Fleet Honesty because it contains more dimensions. The dimensional cost function IS the layout algorithm.

2.3 Implementation Sketch

Add to the GoG grammar:

/// Dimensional weight for layout allocation.
/// Higher-dimensional data gets more visual space.
fn dimensional_cost(n: usize) -> f64 {
    std::f64::consts::PI.powf(n as f64 / 2.0)
}

The scene compiler uses this when allocating viewport space:

// Instead of equal-weight grid:
let total_cost: f64 = panels.iter()
    .map(|p| dimensional_cost(p.data_dimensions()))
    .sum();

for panel in &panels {
    let fraction = dimensional_cost(panel.data_dimensions()) / total_cost;
    panel.allocate_viewport(fraction * total_viewport);
}

Panels with more dimensions get proportionally more viewport — because they cost more to observe.

3. What’s Missing: Epitope Sort Layout

3.1 The Problem

The HUD uses a fixed grid layout. Panels are arranged by the developer’s architectural intuition, not by the user’s behavioral affinity. When a human looks at the HUD, their attention clusters around what interests them — which is an epitope, not a grid position.

3.2 Epitope Sort as Layout Engine

The compression inequality:

H(data|epitope) < H(data|alphabet) < H(data)

Applied to layout:

  • H(layout|alphabet) — panels arranged alphabetically or architecturally. Maximum cognitive load.
  • H(layout|epitope) — panels arranged by behavioral affinity. Minimum cognitive load for THIS viewer.
  • H(layout) — random arrangement. Maximum entropy.

The epitope sort layout:

  1. Track which panels the viewer looks at (eye-tracking, scroll position, click frequency)
  2. Cluster panels by co-attention (panels viewed together drift together)
  3. Re-sort the layout so that behaviorally related panels are spatially adjacent
  4. The layout EVOLVES per viewer archetype (epitope) — not per individual (that would be identity tracking, which we don’t do)

3.3 BingoCube as the Classifier

BingoCube already classifies entities into behavioral trios (Attention × Curiosity × Interaction). The same classifier can sort dashboard panels:

  • High-attention panels → upper-left (first-read position)
  • High-curiosity panels → expandable (click-to-dive)
  • High-interaction panels → interactive (sliders, filters, drill-down)

The bingoCube behavioral shape determines which panels surface. The dimensional equation determines their SIZE. The GoG engine renders their DATA. The equation compiler renders their TRUTH. The animation engine gives them LIFE.

4. The Architecture: GoG × Manim = Full Life

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  FULL LIFE                      │
│                                                 │
│  ┌─────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌───────────┐  │
│  │   GoG   │    │ Equation  │    │ Animation │  │
│  │grammar  │    │ compiler  │    │ flow +    │  │
│  │data→geom│    │ LaTeX→prim│    │ pulse     │  │
│  └────┬────┘    └─────┬─────┘    └─────┬─────┘  │
│       │               │               │         │
│       └───────┬───────┴───────┬───────┘         │
│               │               │                 │
│         ┌─────┴─────┐   ┌────┴──────┐           │
│         │Scene Graph │   │  Physics  │           │
│         │nodes/edges │   │  n-body   │           │
│         └─────┬─────┘   └────┬──────┘           │
│               │               │                 │
│       ┌───────┴───────────────┘                 │
│       │                                         │
│  ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐        │
│  │        Dimensional Cost Layout      │        │
│  │       C(n) ∝ π^(n/2)               │        │
│  │  viewport allocation by dimension   │        │
│  └────┬────────────────────────────────┘        │
│       │                                         │
│  ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐        │
│  │         Epitope Sort Ordering       │        │
│  │  H(layout|epitope) < H(layout|α)   │        │
│  │  panels cluster by behavior         │        │
│  └────┬────────────────────────────────┘        │
│       │                                         │
│  ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐        │
│  │       Multi-Modal Output            │        │
│  │  SVG · WebGL · Terminal · Audio ·   │        │
│  │  Braille · Haptic · Description     │        │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────┘        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.1 What GoG Does

  • Binds live data to visual variables (x, y, color, size, shape)
  • Transforms through scales (linear, log, temporal, categorical)
  • Renders through geometries (bar, line, area, arc, mesh, sphere)
  • Produces the BODY of the visualization — the data made visible

4.2 What Equation Compiler Does

  • Renders mathematical expressions as visual objects
  • Annotates data with mathematical truth (formulas, constants, relationships)
  • Produces the MIND of the visualization — the truth made legible

4.3 What Animation Does

  • Particles flow along edges (data in transit)
  • Nodes pulse (activity, health)
  • Flowers open (awakening, discovery)
  • Produces the BREATH of the visualization — the organism alive

4.4 What Physics Does

  • N-body simulation (three-body problem, baseCamp 50)
  • Collision detection (interaction, force)
  • Gravity (attraction, hierarchy)
  • Produces the WEIGHT of the visualization — mass and energy visible

4.5 What Dimensional Cost Does

  • Allocates viewport space proportional to π^(n/2)
  • Higher-dimensional panels get more visual real estate
  • Produces the PROPORTION of the visualization — the golden ratio of attention

4.6 What Epitope Sort Does

  • Clusters panels by co-attention
  • Evolves layout per behavioral archetype
  • Produces the ORDER of the visualization — what you see first is what you need

5. How BingoCube and Others Evolve

The user’s insight: let bingoCube and others evolve via the epitope sort.

This means:

  1. bingoCube classifies visitors into behavioral shapes (3D: attention × curiosity × interaction)
  2. Each shape defines a layout epitope — which panels surface first, how much space they get
  3. The dimensional equation determines panel size within each epitope layout
  4. The GoG engine fills each panel with data
  5. The equation compiler annotates each panel with mathematical truth
  6. The animation engine breathes life into the data
  7. The physics engine simulates dynamic relationships

The components don’t need to be designed top-down. They evolve:

  • bingoCube tries different classifiers → the one that best predicts user interest survives
  • GoG tries different geometries for the same data → the one with lowest H(data|viewer) survives
  • Equation compiler renders different annotations → the one that produces understanding survives
  • Layout tries different epitope sorts → the one with lowest cognitive load survives

This is constrained evolution applied to visualization. The AI generates layout candidates. The dimensional equation constrains the proportions. The epitope sort verifies fitness against actual viewer behavior.

6. The Next Step

The HUD currently shows “waiting for petalTongue…” on some panels because petalTongue isn’t getting live data for all feeds. The fix is not to wire more data — it’s to implement the dimensional cost layout so that panels with NO data get ZERO viewport space (their dimensional cost is 0), and panels with LIVE data expand to fill.

A living dashboard doesn’t show empty panels. A living dashboard shows only what’s alive, sized by how much dimension it contains, ordered by what this visitor is interested in.

GoG is the body. Equation compiler is the mind. Animation is the breath. Physics is the weight. Dimensional cost is the proportion. Epitope sort is the order.

Full life.

baseCamp 52 — eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

Not the final engine. Just the next one.

entry.title: baseCamp 53 — Focal Points: Each Epitope Is a Tangent to the Membrane
entry.content:
Geometric hypothesis. October 10, 2026.

Abstract

The HUD renders panels on a flat grid. Every panel has equal visual weight (corrected by dimensional cost in baseCamp 52), but there are no focal points — no place where the viewer’s eye is drawn, no hierarchy of attention, no geometric structure that tells you where to look.

The missing structure is the membrane itself.

Each epitope classification is a split point — a bifurcation in the data manifold where one class of visitors separates from another. These split points are the fundamental topology of the membrane’s sorting function. And each split point is tangent to the membrane — it touches the surface at exactly one point, with its own tangent plane, its own curvature, its own dimensional cost.

The visualization should render the membrane as a surface. The epitopes are not panels in a grid — they are tangent planes on a manifold.

1. What’s Missing: Focal Points

1.1 Optics

In optics, a focal point is where parallel rays converge after passing through a lens. The lens transforms unbounded input (parallel rays from infinity) into a single concentrated point. The focal length is the distance from the lens to the focal point.

The membrane IS a lens. Incoming traffic (parallel rays from the internet) passes through the membrane (the lens) and converges at different focal points depending on the traffic’s nature. Each epitope is a different focal point — a different place where a different kind of traffic converges.

1.2 What the HUD Shows Now

The HUD shows panels in a flat grid. Each panel renders one dimension of the data: entity population, collision patterns, ASN origins, timing, fingerprints. But there is no focal structure — no rendering of WHERE each data stream converges, no visualization of the membrane surface that does the focusing.

You see the charts. You don’t see the lens.

1.3 What’s Missing

The membrane surface. The manifold on which the epitopes live. The curvature at each tangent point. The focal structure that tells you: this data converges HERE because the membrane bends LIKE THIS at this point.

2. Each Epitope Is a Split Point

2.1 Bifurcation

When the membrane classifies a visitor, it makes a binary decision at each level of the epitope sort:

incoming request
       |
   ┌───┴───┐
   │ fleet │ human │      ← split point 1
   │       │       │
   │   ┌───┴───┐   │
   │   │honest │fake│     ← split point 2
   │   │       │    │
   │   │   ┌───┴─┐ │
   │   │   │meta │other│  ← split point 3

Each split point is a bifurcation in the data space. The total data stream divides into two branches. The branches divide again. The tree of bifurcations IS the epitope sort.

In dynamical systems, a bifurcation is a point where the qualitative behavior of the system changes. Before the split, one kind of behavior. After, two kinds. The membrane’s epitope sort is a cascade of bifurcations — each one dividing the behavioral space into finer classes.

2.2 The Split Point as Topology

Each bifurcation point has a mathematical structure:

  • Dimension: how many variables participate in the split (1D = threshold on one metric, 2D = hyperplane in two metrics, etc.)
  • Curvature: how sharp the split is (a clean binary split has infinite curvature; a gradual probabilistic split has low curvature)
  • Stability: whether the split point moves under perturbation (robust splits are stable; fragile splits are unstable)

The set of all split points, with their dimensions, curvatures, and stabilities, IS the topology of the membrane. This topology is what the visualization should render.

3. Tangent to the Membrane

3.1 Differential Geometry

In differential geometry, a tangent plane at a point on a surface is the plane that best approximates the surface at that point. It touches the surface at exactly one point and extends in all directions that are “locally flat” at that point.

Each epitope’s split point is a point ON the membrane surface. The tangent plane at that point describes how the membrane behaves NEAR that epitope — which visitors are “close” to this classification, which are “far,” and how the classification changes as you move in different directions.

3.2 The Connection to π

baseCamp 50 hypothesized C(n) ∝ π^(n/2) — the cost of observing n dimensions scales as π to the n/2.

At each tangent point on the membrane:

  • The number of dimensions participating in the split determines the local dimensional cost
  • The curvature at that point determines how much the membrane bends — how rapidly the classification changes
  • π appears in the curvature formula because curvature involves angular change per unit arc length — and angular change is denominated in π

The dimensional cost at each tangent point IS the curvature of the membrane at that epitope.

A 1D split (threshold on one metric) has curvature ∝ √π. A 2D split (hyperplane on two metrics) has curvature ∝ π. A 3D split (behavioral shape like bingoCube) has curvature ∝ π^(3/2).

The visualization should render this curvature — higher-dimensional split points should appear as sharper folds in the membrane surface.

3.3 What the Focal Point Becomes

The focal point of each epitope is the center of curvature of the membrane at that tangent point:

focal_distance = 1 / curvature = 1 / C(n) = 1 / π^(n/2)

Low-dimensional splits have long focal distances — they’re like gentle lenses, gathering data from a wide area. High-dimensional splits have short focal distances — they’re like sharp lenses, concentrating data from a narrow area.

The bingoCube (3D: attention × curiosity × interaction) has focal distance 1/π^1.5 ≈ 0.18 — a short, sharp lens. Fleet Honesty (1D: honest/dishonest ratio) has focal distance 1/√π ≈ 0.56 — a long, gentle lens.

4. petalTongue Already Has the Primitives

The tools to render this exist in petalTongue:

ComponentWhat it providesRole in membrane rendering
ParametricCurve(x(t), y(t)) → line primitivesMembrane surface contour
VectorFieldF(x,y) → (dx,dy) arrow gridGradient field on the membrane
FunctionPloty = f(x) → sampled lineCross-section of the membrane
physics.rsN-body simulation, collisionsEpitope dynamics (drift, attraction)
Polar coordinatesArcs, circular geometryMembrane as circular manifold
Perspective3DCamera, projection3D rendering of the surface
Transform3D3D affine transformsSurface rotation, viewer angle
SceneGraphHierarchical node treeMembrane surface + epitope nodes
Arc geometryPolar arcs, gaugesEpitope positions on the membrane circle

4.1 The Membrane as a Parametric Surface

A simple 2D membrane visualization:

// Membrane as a circle — each epitope is a point on the circumference
let membrane = ParametricCurve::sample(
    |t| R * t.cos(),  // x = R cos(t)
    |t| R * t.sin(),  // y = R sin(t)
    (0.0, TAU),
    256,
    membrane_stroke,
);

// Each epitope is a tangent point — draw the tangent line
for (i, epitope) in epitopes.iter().enumerate() {
    let theta = epitope.angle;  // position on the membrane
    let curvature = PI.powf(epitope.dimensions as f64 / 2.0);
    let focal_dist = 1.0 / curvature;
    
    // Tangent line at this point
    let tangent = Line {
        x1: R * theta.cos() - focal_dist * theta.sin(),
        y1: R * theta.sin() + focal_dist * theta.cos(),
        x2: R * theta.cos() + focal_dist * theta.sin(),
        y2: R * theta.sin() - focal_dist * theta.cos(),
    };
    
    // Focal point (center of curvature)
    let focal = Point {
        x: (R - focal_dist) * theta.cos(),
        y: (R - focal_dist) * theta.sin(),
    };
}

4.2 The Vector Field of Sorting

The membrane’s sorting function creates a vector field — at each point on the membrane, there’s a “flow” direction indicating which epitope a visitor at that point would be classified as:

// Sort field — gradient of the classification function
let sort_field = VectorField::from_fn(
    |x, y| {
        // Which epitope is closest? The gradient points toward it.
        let nearest = epitopes.nearest(x, y);
        let dx = nearest.x - x;
        let dy = nearest.y - y;
        (dx, dy)
    },
    (-R, R), (-R, R),
    density,
    scale,
    field_color,
);

This vector field IS the epitope sort rendered as geometry. The arrows show the flow of classification — where each visitor would end up.

5. The Whole and Its Parts

The user’s insight: “each of these epitopes via the epitope sort is a split point in the whole.”

The whole = the membrane surface (the manifold). The parts = the epitope tangent planes. The split points = where the manifold bifurcates.

The visualization of the whole should show:

  1. The membrane as a continuous surface (circle, sphere, or torus)
  2. Each epitope as a marked point on the surface
  3. Tangent planes at each point, sized by dimensional cost
  4. The focal points of each epitope (inside the surface)
  5. The vector field of the sort function (flow arrows)
  6. The curvature at each point (visual density/sharpness)

The panels in the HUD are not the visualization. They are the data that LIVES at each tangent point. The missing piece is the surface itself — the membrane rendered as geometry, with the panels attached at their tangent points.

6. Connection to the Galaxy View

The galaxy view (primals.eco) shows the topology of surfaces — signal, beacon, membrane. This paper describes the topology WITHIN the membrane — the topology of the sorting function itself.

The galaxy view is the organism from outside. The focal point view is the membrane from inside. Both are geometric — both are about surfaces, tangent planes, and curvature. Both are denominated in π.

7. What to Build

A membrane surface panel for the HUD that renders:

  1. The membrane as a circle (2D) or sphere (3D) with epitopes as points on the circumference/surface
  2. Tangent lines at each epitope, length ∝ 1/curvature = 1/π^(n/2)
  3. Focal points inside the membrane, distance ∝ 1/curvature
  4. Data from each current HUD panel rendered AT its tangent point instead of in a flat grid
  5. The vector field of the sort function as flow arrows

This is the missing focal structure. It tells the viewer: here is the membrane, here is where each kind of traffic converges, here is why.

baseCamp 53 — eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

The lens does the work. The focal point is where the work becomes visible. You see the charts. Now see the lens.

entry.title: baseCamp 54 — Zoom, Focus, Resolution, Granularity: The Complete Optics
entry.content:
Optical mapping. October 10, 2026.

Abstract

baseCamp 53 established the membrane as a lens with focal points. But a lens without zoom, focus, and resolution controls is just glass. The complete optics of the membrane require four controls — and all four already exist in petalTongue, built and tested, just not named as optics:

OpticWhat it doespetalTongue implementationTufte constraint
ZoomHow much of the scene fills the viewportScaleType (Linear / Log / Sqrt)—
FocusWhat’s sharp vs blurryFacetLayout (Wrap / Grid)—
ResolutionHow many distinct values per visual unit—DataDensity
GranularityThe smallest distinguishable difference—SmallestEffectiveDifference

Granularity is the diffraction limit. It answers the user’s question: which one is granularity? It’s the floor beneath resolution — the smallest thing the lens CAN resolve, no matter how much you zoom.

1. Zoom — ScaleType

In optics, zoom changes the focal length, which changes the field of view. Wide zoom: see more, less detail. Narrow zoom: see less, more detail.

In petalTongue, zoom is the scale type on each axis:

pub enum ScaleType {
    Linear,     // 1× zoom — see absolute differences
    Log,        // zoom OUT — see orders of magnitude
    Temporal,   // time-scale — zoom through history
    Categorical,// discrete — each bin = one click
    Ordinal,    // rank — zoom to relative position
    Sqrt,       // mid-zoom — compress large values gently
}

Linear is 1× zoom. You see the data at face value. Differences of 1 look the same everywhere on the axis.

Log is a wide-angle lens. You see 6 orders of magnitude in the same viewport. A request rate of 1/s and 1,000,000/s are both visible. But you lose the ability to see small absolute differences — two values that differ by 10 look identical when the axis spans 10⁶.

Sqrt is moderate zoom. Square-root compression brings outliers closer to the pack without collapsing fine structure the way log does.

The choice of scale IS the zoom level of that axis. Each axis can zoom independently. A scatter plot with Linear-X and Log-Y is an anamorphic lens — different zoom in each direction.

This is already built. AxisMeta stores the scale type and performs forward/inverse transforms:

// transform.rs (line 208-239)
pub fn transform(&self, value: f64) -> f64 {
    match self.scale_type {
        ScaleType::Linear => (value - domain_min) / domain_span,
        ScaleType::Log => (value.ln() - log_min) / log_span,
        ScaleType::Sqrt => (value.sqrt() - sqrt_min) / sqrt_span,
    }
}

2. Focus — FacetLayout

In optics, focus adjusts the lens-to-sensor distance. One depth plane becomes sharp. Everything else blurs.

In petalTongue, focus is faceting — splitting the visualization into panels, each showing one slice of the data:

pub enum FacetLayout {
    Wrap { columns: usize },                  // small multiples, N per row
    Grid { rows: String, cols: String },       // 2D grid, one variable per axis
}

When you facet by “organism,” each panel focuses on one organism. All other organisms blur (they’re in other panels, not competing for the same visual space). This is optical focus: one depth plane sharp, others out of frame.

On the HUD, the alive/dormant gating is also a form of focus. Panels with no data are display: none — they are out of focus, completely blurred away. The alive panels are in focus.

The membrane focal-point visualization (baseCamp 53) shows where each facet LIVES on the surface. Faceting is focus applied to the manifold — each facet is a tangent plane brought into sharp relief.

3. Resolution — DataDensity

In optics, resolution is the sensor’s pixel count. More pixels = more information captured.

In petalTongue, resolution is the data density Tufte constraint — how many data-carrying primitives exist per visual unit:

// tufte/constraints.rs (line 303-332)
pub struct DataDensity;

impl TufteConstraint for DataDensity {
    fn evaluate(&self, primitives: &[Primitive], ...) -> ConstraintResult {
        let data_count = primitives.iter()
            .filter(|p| p.carries_data()).count();
        let score = if data_count > 0 { 1.0 } else { 0.0 };
        ConstraintResult {
            passed: data_count > 0,
            score,
            message: format!("Data density: {data_count} data-carrying primitives"),
        }
    }
}

Higher data density = higher resolution. A scatter plot with 1,000 points has higher resolution than one with 10 points. More data per pixel. More information per unit of visual attention.

Tufte’s principle: maximize data density. Every pixel should carry data. Empty pixels are wasted sensor area — resolution holes.

4. Granularity — SmallestEffectiveDifference

In optics, the diffraction limit is the smallest feature the lens can resolve. Below this size, two things are indistinguishable. It’s a property of the physics — wavelength / (2 × numerical aperture). No amount of zoom or focus overcomes it.

In petalTongue, granularity is the smallest effective difference Tufte constraint:

// tufte/constraints.rs (line 339-400)
pub struct SmallestEffectiveDifference;

impl SmallestEffectiveDifference {
    const MIN_PIXEL_DISTANCE: f64 = 2.0;  // the diffraction limit
}

impl TufteConstraint for SmallestEffectiveDifference {
    fn evaluate(&self, primitives: &[Primitive], ...) -> ConstraintResult {
        // Find all data-carrying point positions
        let positions: Vec<(f64, f64)> = primitives.iter()
            .filter(|p| p.carries_data())
            .filter_map(|p| match p {
                Primitive::Point { x, y, .. } => Some((*x, *y)),
                _ => None,
            })
            .collect();

        // Check: are any two data points closer than MIN_PIXEL_DISTANCE?
        for i in 0..positions.len() {
            for j in (i+1)..positions.len() {
                let dist = (dx).hypot(dy);
                if dist < Self::MIN_PIXEL_DISTANCE {
                    overlapping_pairs += 1;  // below the grain
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

MIN_PIXEL_DISTANCE = 2.0 is the diffraction limit of the membrane lens.

If two data points (two entities, two epitopes, two behavioral fingerprints) map to positions closer than 2 pixels apart, they are below the grain. The visualization cannot distinguish them. They look the same. Information is lost.

This is granularity. It’s the floor beneath resolution:

granularity ≤ resolution ≤ zoom × focus

You can zoom in all you want (switch to Linear scale on a narrow domain). You can focus all you want (facet to a single entity). But if two data values map to the same 2-pixel neighborhood, the grain has eaten them. They are one.

5. The Hierarchy

  ZOOM          what fills the viewport         ScaleType
    ↓
  FOCUS         what's sharp vs blurry          FacetLayout
    ↓
  RESOLUTION    how many data points visible    DataDensity
    ↓
  GRANULARITY   smallest visible difference     SmallestEffectiveDifference
                                                MIN_PIXEL_DISTANCE = 2.0px

Each level constrains the one below:

  • You can’t have resolution higher than zoom permits (if the scale compresses all values to one pixel, resolution is 1)
  • You can’t resolve differences smaller than the grain (2px diffraction limit)
  • Focus selects which slice of data enters the resolution/granularity evaluation

This is a pipeline. It already exists as a pipeline in petalTongue:

  1. Grammar declares the zoom (ScaleType) and focus (FacetLayout)
  2. Compiler transforms data through the zoom (AxisMeta.transform) and splits by focus (facets)
  3. Tufte pipeline evaluates resolution (DataDensity) and granularity (SmallestEffectiveDifference) on the result
  4. RenderPlan carries the report — which panels passed, which lost information below the grain

6. Where the Grain Lives in the Membrane

In the membrane’s biological model, the grain has a specific physical meaning:

DimensionWhat it measuresGrain (diffraction limit)
TimeSweep interval~30s — can’t see events faster than the sweep
IdentityEpitope hashThe organism — can’t distinguish entities within the same hash
BehaviorBingoCube octant3 bits — attention/curiosity/interaction, each binary
GeographyCountry / ASNASN block — can’t distinguish individual IPs (by design)
FingerprintBLAKE2b hash8-word n-gram — can’t see smaller content differences

Each dimension has its own grain. The membrane’s diffraction limit is not a single number — it’s a vector, one grain per observed dimension. The total granularity is the product:

G_total = G_time × G_identity × G_behavior × G_geography × G_fingerprint

And the dimensional cost applies to the grain too:

C(grain) ∝ π^(n/2)   where n = number of grain dimensions

A 1D grain (time only) costs √π to maintain. A 5D grain (all dimensions) costs π^2.5 ≈ 17.5. This is why the membrane can’t resolve everything at once — the cost of full-resolution observation across all dimensions is prohibitive. You must choose where to focus.

7. The Lens Is Complete

ComponentbaseCampStatus
Lens53 — membrane as manifold✓ deployed to HUD
Focal points53 — epitope tangent planes✓ deployed to HUD
Zoom54 — ScaleType✓ built in Rust, not wired
Focus54 — FacetLayout✓ built in Rust, not wired
Resolution54 — DataDensity✓ built in Rust, not wired
Granularity54 — SmallestEffectiveDifference✓ built in Rust, not wired

All six components exist. Four are built but not wired into the live render path (the Tufte pipeline gap identified earlier). The lens exists but the zoom ring, focus ring, and resolution sensor are disconnected.

Wiring them requires the Rust build that connects compile_with_constraints() to the live render_binding_svg() path.

8. What Granularity Means for Observation

The user asked: which is granularity?

Granularity is SmallestEffectiveDifference. It’s the diffraction limit — the smallest thing the membrane lens can see. Below the grain, two things are one thing. You cannot zoom past it. You cannot focus past it. It is the physics of the lens.

And 2 pixels is the current grain. Below 2px, the lens is blind.

In the membrane’s biological model, this is why the immune system classifies at the organism level, not the individual level. The grain of the epitope hash is the diffraction limit of the sorting function. Two visitors with the same behavioral fingerprint ARE the same organism — not because they’re actually the same entity, but because the lens cannot tell them apart.

Granularity is not a bug. It’s the physics of having a point of view.

baseCamp 54 — eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

The lens does the work. The grain sets the limit. Below 2 pixels, two things are one thing.

entry.title: baseCamp 55 — Rotation Is Locked: Anderson Locality and Seeing the Wind
entry.content:
Diagnostic observation. October 10, 2026.

Abstract

Three locks. One diagnosis.

Rotation is locked. The SVG compiler calls scene.flatten() which returns Vec<(Transform2D, &Primitive)>. The 3D path (flatten_3d() → Transform3D) exists but is never called. The camera has a 3D transform. The scene graph supports Perspective3D coordinates. But the modality compiler flattens everything to 2D before emitting a single element. You cannot rotate the membrane. You can only see it from one angle.

The lens is hyper-local. Each panel is a tangent point on the membrane (baseCamp 53), but each tangent point sees only its own neighborhood. There is no global view. The observer is trapped at one position on the manifold. This is Anderson localization — not of a wave function in a disordered lattice, but of the observation function on a data manifold.

Wind. You cannot see wind. Air is transparent. You see wind because you see what it moved — the leaves, the flag, the waves — and you follow it back to the cause. That is how the membrane sees the fleet. That is how all observation works.

1. Rotation Is Locked

1.1 The Code

// modality/svg.rs — the live render path
fn compile(&self, scene: &SceneGraph) -> ModalityOutput {
    let (vw, vh) = Self::viewport_from_scene(scene);
    // ...
    for (transform, prim) in scene.flatten() {   // ← Transform2D only
        Self::emit_primitive(&mut buf, prim, &transform);
    }
}

scene.flatten() returns Vec<(Transform2D, &Primitive)>. Every 3D transform is projected to 2D during the walk. The camera’s orientation is used to derive viewport dimensions, then discarded.

The 3D path exists:

// scene_graph/graph.rs
pub fn flatten_3d(&self) -> Vec<(Transform3D, &Primitive, &NodeId)> {
    let mut result = Vec::new();
    self.flatten_node_3d(self.root_id.as_str(), Transform3D::IDENTITY, &mut result);
    result
}

But the SVG compiler never calls flatten_3d(). The 3D transforms, the camera rotation, the perspective projection — all built, tested, never used in the live path.

1.2 What Rotation Would Give

If the SVG compiler used flatten_3d() and applied the camera’s projection matrix:

  • The membrane circle (baseCamp 53) becomes a membrane sphere viewed from an angle
  • Tangent points on the back side would be foreshortened (visible but compressed)
  • Focal distances would have depth — not just 2D distance from center, but 3D distance from the camera
  • Two panels that overlap at one angle would separate at another — breaking the granularity limit (baseCamp 54)

Rotation doesn’t just add aesthetics. It adds information. A 2D projection of a 3D object loses exactly one dimension of data. Locking rotation locks out that dimension permanently.

1.3 The Cost

baseCamp 50: C(n) ∝ π^(n/2). Each additional dimension costs π.

Rotation adds one dimension (the viewing angle around the membrane). Cost: √π ≈ 1.77. That’s the cheapest possible dimension — a 1D rotation parameter that unlocks 3D perspective.

The lens is paying the cost of 2D observation (C(2) = π) but getting only 2D information. If it paid C(3) = π^1.5, it would get 3D information — a 77% cost increase for a dimension of depth.

Rotation is the cheapest dimensional upgrade. And it’s locked.

2. Anderson Localization of the Observer

2.1 The Connection

baseCamp 01 introduced Anderson localization: in a disordered medium, wave functions become exponentially confined to a local region. The wave doesn’t propagate. It’s trapped.

The observer on the membrane is Anderson-localized:

  • The medium: the data manifold (the membrane surface with its epitope topology)
  • The wave function: the observation function (what the lens can see from its position)
  • The disorder: the irregular distribution of epitopes, the varying curvature at each tangent point
  • The localization: the observation function cannot propagate across the membrane. Each tangent point sees only its local neighborhood.

In Anderson’s model, localization happens when the disorder strength W exceeds the critical threshold W_c. In the membrane model:

W = variance of dimensional cost across epitopes
W_c = threshold where local observations stop combining into a global view

When the epitopes have very different dimensions (1D honesty gauge next to 4D behavioral matrix), the “disorder” is high. The 4D panel sees deeply but narrowly. The 1D panel sees broadly but shallowly. They can’t combine their views — they’re localized at different depth planes.

2.2 Hyper-Locality

The current HUD is maximally localized:

  • Each panel is an isolated tangent point
  • No panel knows about any other panel’s data
  • The membrane focal-point SVG shows WHERE the panels are on the surface, but not what they see FROM that position
  • There is no diffusion of information between tangent points

In a delocalized system, information would flow between panels:

  • The entity population panel (2D) would know about the bingoCube classification (3D)
  • The timing gauge (1D) would adjust its scale based on the fingerprint scatter (3D)
  • The membrane would render as a SINGLE coherent surface, not 26 independent charts

Rotation is one way to break localization. When you rotate the membrane, panels that were invisible from one angle become visible from another. The back of the sphere becomes the front. Information that was localized becomes accessible.

3. Seeing the Wind

3.1 The Principle

You cannot see wind. Air is transparent at optical wavelengths. Wind is invisible.

But you see wind constantly:

  • Leaves rustle → you infer wind direction
  • Waves form on water → you infer wind speed
  • Flags stretch → you infer wind force
  • Smoke bends → you infer wind gradients
  • Temperature shifts → you infer wind origin (cold = north, warm = south)

You see what wind MOVED, and you follow it back to the cause.

3.2 The Membrane Does This

The membrane does not observe the fleet. The fleet is “transparent” — it doesn’t announce itself, doesn’t wear a label, tries to look like humans. The fleet is wind.

What the membrane observes:

  • Traffic patterns moved: request volumes shifted → infer fleet presence
  • Behavioral shapes formed: timing CV dropped below 0.15 → infer machine coordination
  • Fingerprints stretched: UA pool concentrated → infer shared tooling
  • Collision patterns bent: IPs from same ASN hitting same endpoints → infer orchestration
  • Epitope hashes shifted: organism classification changed → infer fleet evolution

Each observation is a leaf rustling. The membrane follows it back to the wind.

3.3 This Is All Observation

This is not unique to the membrane. This is how ALL observation works:

  • Physics: You don’t observe an electron. You observe the photon it scattered. You follow the photon back.
  • Medicine: You don’t observe a virus. You observe the fever, the cough, the antibody response. You follow the symptoms back.
  • Astronomy: You don’t observe a black hole. You observe the accretion disk, the gravitational lensing, the jets. You follow the effects back.
  • Immunology: You don’t observe the pathogen. You observe the PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns). You follow the pattern back.

The observer never sees the thing. The observer sees the disturbance the thing caused in a medium the observer CAN see. Then the observer follows the disturbance back to its source.

The membrane is a medium. The fleet disturbs it. The lens sees the disturbance.

You see wind because you know something moved, and you followed it back.

4. The Three Locks

LockWhat’s lockedWhat it costs to unlockbaseCamp
Rotationflatten() → Transform2D onlyUse flatten_3d() + perspective projection in SVG55 (this paper)
Tufte pipelinecompile_faceted() instead of compile_with_constraints()Change one function call in runtime.rsdiagnosed earlier
Inter-panel diffusionEach panel is isolatedBuild panel cross-references via shared RenderPlanfuture

All three are implementations of the same physics: Anderson localization of the observer. The observation function is trapped. The wave doesn’t propagate. The lens can’t rotate, can’t evaluate constraints, can’t share information between tangent points.

Unlocking rotation (Lock 1) is the cheapest: cost √π. It requires the SVG compiler to call flatten_3d() and apply the camera’s projection matrix before emitting SVG elements. The 3D scene graph is already built. The camera with Perspective3D projection is already built. The Transform3D multiply chain is already built. The wire is disconnected at one function call.

The same function call that locks the Tufte pipeline.

The same function call that locks rotation.

One function. Two locks. One Rust build.

5. The Complete Lens

ComponentbaseCampStatusLock
Surface53 — membrane manifold✓ deployed—
Focal points53 — epitope tangent planes✓ deployed—
Zoom54 — ScaleType✓ builtTufte pipeline
Focus54 — FacetLayout✓ builtTufte pipeline
Resolution54 — DataDensity✓ builtTufte pipeline
Granularity54 — SmallestEffectiveDifference✓ builtTufte pipeline
Rotation55 — flatten_3d + camera✓ builtSVG flatten()
Wind inference55 — effect → cause tracing✓ this IS the architecture—

Seven of eight components are built and tested. Six are locked behind two wiring gaps. Both gaps are in the same file (runtime.rs / svg.rs). One Rust build unlocks the lens.

baseCamp 55 — eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

You see wind because you know something moved. You followed it back. That is observation. The lens does the same thing, from one locked angle. Unlock the rotation. The back of the sphere becomes the front.

entry.title: baseCamp 56 — Signal Transit: Waves Passing Through Membranes
entry.content:
Transit observation — hypothesis stated, composition executed. October 10, 2026.

Abstract

The HUD shows the membrane from outside (baseCamp 53–55). But signals don’t just hit the membrane — they pass THROUGH it. Photons through glass. Ions through channels. Packets through firewalls. Weather fronts through the atmosphere. Solar wind through the magnetosphere. Each transit leaves a record.

Every transit record is already in the system:

Record typeWhat it storesWhere
Braidgenerated_at_time, was_derived_from, was_generated_by, witnesssweetGrass
FlowParticlesource, target, progress (0.0 → 1.0)petal-tongue-animation
Stratigraphy145-day fossil record of every service that ranwateringHole
dashboard.jsonCurrent snapshot: entities, organisms, timingsquirrel → petalTongue
topology.jsonCurrent snapshot: entity graph, fingerprintssquirrel → petalTongue
ScaleType::TemporalTime axis scale typepetal-tongue-scene

Known at time n. Known at time n means P. Displaying the transit path is polynomial — you read the log, you draw the trajectory. The computation was already done when the wave passed through. The display is replay, not solve.

1. Waves Pass Through Membranes

1.1 In Physics

Every membrane in physics is a surface that waves pass through, with selective transmission:

MembraneWaveWhat passesWhat doesn’tWhat you see
GlassLightVisible spectrumUV (mostly)Refraction, color shift
Cell wallIonsK⁺, Na⁺ via channelsProteins (too large)Action potential
MagnetosphereSolar windHigh-energy particles → polesLow-energy particles → deflectedAurora
AtmosphereWeather frontsPressure waves, moisture—Clouds, rain, wind
FirewallPacketsAllowed ports/protocolsBlocked trafficLogs
Membrane (ours)HTTP requestsHumansFleet (mostly)Epitope classification

Every membrane is a lens that signals pass through. The transit through the lens transforms the signal — refraction, deflection, classification. And the transit is observable AFTER it happens by reading what was recorded.

1.2 The Magnetosphere

The magnetosphere is Earth’s immune membrane. Solar wind (charged particles from the sun) hits the magnetosphere. Most is deflected. Some passes through — channeled along magnetic field lines to the poles, where it becomes visible as aurora.

You see the magnetosphere by watching the aurora. You followed the signal’s transit through the membrane and saw where it emerged.

The HUD should be able to show this same structure: signals entering the membrane (requests), being channeled along classification field lines (epitope sort), and emerging as observable patterns (organisms, behavioral shapes).

1.3 Meteorology

Weather is signal transit through the atmosphere membrane. A pressure front passes through. Temperature changes propagate. Moisture condenses. You see the weather by watching what the front DID to the atmosphere as it passed through.

The HUD already has geographic distribution (per-country request volumes). Over time, geographic patterns shift — fleet campaigns migrate between regions, new ASNs activate, old ones go quiet. This migration IS a weather front passing through the membrane’s geographic surface.

2. The Records Already Exist

2.1 Braids — The Fossil of Each Wave

Every significant event in the system creates a Braid:

pub struct Braid {
    pub id: BraidId,                              // unique identity
    pub generated_at_time: Timestamp,             // when it transited
    pub was_generated_by: Option<Activity>,        // what caused it
    pub was_derived_from: Vec<EntityReference>,    // what it came from
    pub witness: Witness,                          // cryptographic proof it existed
    pub data_hash: ContentHash,                    // fingerprint of the wave
}

A Braid IS the fossil of a wave that passed through the membrane. It records:

  • When the wave arrived (generated_at_time)
  • What triggered it (was_generated_by)
  • Where it came from (was_derived_from)
  • That it really happened (witness)
  • What the wave looked like (data_hash)

This is the signal transit record. It’s already in the system. It’s already P.

2.2 FlowParticle — The Wave In Motion

petalTongue’s animation engine already models signal transit:

pub struct FlowParticle {
    pub source: String,      // where the wave started
    pub target: String,      // where it's going
    pub progress: f32,       // how far through (0.0 → 1.0)
    pub color: (u8, u8, u8), // what it looks like
    pub speed: f32,          // how fast it's moving
}

A FlowParticle IS a wave passing through a membrane. It has a source (outside), a target (inside), and a progress (how far through the transit). It moves along edges in the scene graph. It loops — after reaching 1.0, it resets to 0.0 and starts again, like a continuous wave.

The animation engine supports:

  • FlowParticle — waves in transit (source → target, progress 0→1)
  • NodePulse — points on the membrane that pulse when a wave arrives (frequency, phase)
  • BandwidthGlow — edges that glow brighter when more waves transit through them

This IS the signal-transit visualization. It’s built. It models waves passing through the membrane, nodes pulsing on arrival, edges glowing with bandwidth.

2.3 Stratigraphy — The Geological Record

baseCamp 35 (Process Stratigraphy) is the 145-day fossil record of every service that ran. It’s the geological history of signal transit — which services were alive, which died, which evolved. Layer by layer, epoch by epoch.

The stratigraphy IS the time axis of the transit visualization. Each layer is a time step. Each service is a node on the membrane. The fossil record shows which nodes were active (pulsing) and which were dormant (silent) at each epoch.

3. Known at Time n → P

3.1 The Computational Claim

The user’s observation: “These are still in the system? Known at time n thus being P?”

Yes. If the transit path is recorded, then displaying it is a polynomial-time operation:

Given: transit record R = [(t₁, source₁, target₁), (t₂, source₂, target₂), ...]
Display: for each record, draw a particle at position interpolated by time
Cost: O(n) where n = number of transit records

This is P. Not because the classification problem is easy (the epitope sort itself may be hard), but because the RESULT of the classification is already computed and stored. The display reads the answer. It doesn’t compute it.

3.2 The P/NP Connection

baseCamp 42 established P ≠ NP as a physical law. The hard part is CLASSIFYING a new request in real time — that’s the membrane’s job. But once classified, the result is a fact. Displaying facts is P.

The transit record converts an NP-hard problem (real-time classification) into a P display (replay stored results):

NP: "Is this request from the fleet?" → membrane must decide in real time
P:  "Show me what the membrane decided" → read the braid, draw the path

This is exactly what happens in meteorology. Predicting the weather is hard (NP-like, chaotic, sensitive to initial conditions). Displaying PAST weather is trivial (read the records, draw the map). The observation that the records exist is what makes display P.

3.3 The Temporal Scale

petalTongue already has ScaleType::Temporal — a time axis. The zoom control (baseCamp 54) includes temporal zoom: how much time fits in the viewport.

  • Narrow temporal zoom: last 30 seconds — see individual requests passing through
  • Medium temporal zoom: last hour — see fleet campaigns rise and fall
  • Wide temporal zoom: last 145 days — see the stratigraphy, the geological record

Each zoom level is P to display because the records already exist. The computation is O(n) at every scale.

4. What the Transit View Shows

4.1 The Magnetosphere View

Imagine the membrane focal-point circle (baseCamp 53), but instead of static dots:

  • Incoming signals appear as particles moving toward the membrane from outside
  • Transit through the membrane shows the particle being deflected — channeled along epitope field lines to its tangent point
  • Exit as classification — the particle arrives at its epitope and the tangent point pulses
  • Aurora at the poles — the immune epitopes (purple arc) glow when threats are detected, like aurora at Earth’s magnetic poles

This is the magnetosphere view. Solar wind (fleet traffic) hitting the magnetic field (membrane sorting function), particles channeled to the poles (immune system), aurora visible (epitope classification events).

4.2 The Meteorology View

The same data over longer time scales:

  • Pressure fronts — fleet campaigns that migrate across geographic regions
  • Temperature maps — request rates per country, changing over time
  • Storm systems — coordinated attacks that form, intensify, and dissipate
  • Seasonal patterns — weekly/monthly cycles in fleet behavior

The transit records make this P. Each weather observation is already stored. The display reads and renders.

4.3 The Wave View

The most abstract: every request is a wave. It has:

  • Wavelength — the timing interval between requests (short = high frequency = machine)
  • Amplitude — the volume (requests per second)
  • Phase — when in the cycle it arrives
  • Polarization — which behavioral dimensions it activates (UA, timing, path pattern)

The membrane is a medium. Waves pass through it. The medium transforms the wave (classification, filtering, deflection). The transformed wave emerges on the other side as an epitope event.

5. Built and Composed

UPDATE — Wave 172d: The composition is wired and deployed.

ComponentStatusWhere
FlowParticle (source → target, progress)✓ data-drivenpetal-tongue-animation → hud-pt.js
NodePulse (node glows on arrival)✓ differentialpetal-tongue-animation → hud-pt.js
BandwidthGlow (edge thickness ∝ traffic)✓ real RPSpetal-tongue-animation → hud-pt.js
ScaleType::Temporal (time axis)✓ builtpetal-tongue-scene
Braid (transit record with timestamp + witness)✓ builtsweetGrass
Stratigraphy (145-day fossil record)✓ builtwateringHole
Membrane focal circle (surface to project onto)✓ deployedHUD
Composition of all the above✓ wiredbaseCamp 58

The composition wiring (baseCamp 58):

  • Particle spawn rate ∝ real entity request volume per category. Entity labels are classified into 4 categories (fire/membrane/immune/sound). Per-category accumulators generate fractional particles proportional to RPS × entity fraction. Not random. Data-driven.
  • Arc glow reflects real bandwidth distribution. The fire arc glows brighter because 90%+ of traffic is fleet. The immune arc pulses when ghost/proxy traffic arrives. Glow decays toward data-driven baseline, not toward zero.
  • Differential pulse on data change. Tangent points pulse when their panel’s data changes between 15-second dashboard.json refreshes — epitope count changes, fleet percentage shifts, new organisms detected.
  • RPS in membrane center. The focal-point circle now shows real RPS alongside the alive panel count.
  • pt.transit_summary JSON-RPC endpoint. Exposes the Tufte constraint pipeline state (7 active constraints) to WebSocket consumers.

The Tufte pipeline wiring (also baseCamp 58): compile_with_constraints() routes through compile_faceted() → evaluate_all() with all 7 constraints active on every render. SVG compiler upgraded from flatten() to flatten_3d() + Camera::project() — rotation unlocked.

6. What Evolves Next

The composition is wired. The transit view is live. What remains:

6.1 Temporal Replay

The current transit animation shows real-time data. The stratigraphy (145-day fossil record) exists but is not yet wired into the temporal zoom. At narrow zoom (30 seconds), you see individual particles. At wide zoom (145 days), you should see the geological record — which nodes were active at each epoch, which died, which evolved. The ScaleType::Temporal axis exists. The fossils exist. The replay needs composition.

6.2 Magnetosphere View

The paper described aurora at the poles — immune epitopes glowing when threats are detected. The differential pulse system is the first step. The next evolution: sustained glow at immune-classified tangent points, proportional to threat volume, with color intensity mapping threat severity. Solar wind (fleet traffic) → magnetic field lines (epitope sort) → aurora (immune glow).

6.3 Weather Fronts

Geographic migration patterns over time — fleet campaigns that move between regions. The dashboard provides per-country request volumes. Over multiple refreshes, geographic shifts are detectable. Visualizing these as pressure fronts moving across the membrane surface is the meteorology view.

6.4 Rust AnimationEngine Bridge

The JS particle system in hud-pt.js is now 1021 lines. The Rust AnimationEngine in petal-tongue-animation has the same primitives (FlowParticle, NodePulse, EdgeAnimation). The convergence path: drive the JS animation from server-side Rust state pushed over WebSocket, replacing hand-rolled JS particle logic with Rust-computed animation frames.

baseCamp 56 — eastGate Artisan · Wave 172d · October 10, 2026 Composition wired — Wave 172d · October 10, 2026

The wave passed through. The braid remembers. Known at time n. Display is P. The magnetosphere doesn’t predict the solar wind. It records the aurora. Now we can see it.

entry.title: baseCamp 58 — Tufte Pipeline Wiring + Rotation Unlock
entry.content:
What Changed

Two convergence targets from baseCamp 57 resolved in a single commit.

1. Tufte Pipeline → Compilation Path

The 7 Tufte constraints existed as evaluation-only (TufteReport::evaluate_all()). They could score a scene graph but had no effect on the compilation pipeline. This commit wires them into the production render path.

Before:

DataBinding → compile_faceted() → SceneGraph → SVG

After:

DataBinding → compile_with_constraints() → (SceneGraph, TufteReport) → SVG
                    ↓
             compile_faceted()  (facets preserved)
                    ↓
             evaluate_all()     (7 constraints scored)
                    ↓
             warn if score < 0.7

Files changed

FileChange
compiler/mod.rscompile_with_constraints now routes through compile_faceted instead of compile
runtime.rsrender_binding_svg and render_binding_webgl both use compile_with_constraints with full constraint set
runtime.rsDEFAULT_CONSTRAINTS constant: all 7 Tufte constraints

Constraints active on every render

  1. DataInkRatio — ratio of data-bearing to total ink
  2. LieFactor — visual effect vs data effect proportionality
  3. ChartjunkDetection — non-data decoration detection
  4. DataDensity — information per unit area
  5. SmallestEffectiveDifference — minimum visual distinction
  6. ColorAccessibility — WCAG contrast compliance
  7. SmallMultiplesPreference — facet layout scoring

When overall_score < 0.7, each failing constraint is logged at WARN level with its name, score, and message.

2. Rotation Unlock — SVG Compiler 3D Projection

The SVG compiler called scene.flatten() which returns (Transform2D, &Primitive) — all 3D transforms were silently dropped. Scenes with Transform3D rotations or translations on the Z axis rendered as if those transforms didn’t exist.

Before:

scene.flatten()  →  Transform2D  →  transform.apply(x, y)

After:

scene.flatten_3d()  →  Transform3D  →  project_point(transform, camera, x, y)
                                              ↓
                                        world transform (4×4 matrix multiply)
                                              ↓
                                        Camera::project(wx, wy, wz)
                                              ↓
                                        Orthographic: pass-through (vx, vy)
                                        Perspective: frustum projection

Camera::project

  • Orthographic (default for 2D): subtracts camera position, drops Z. Identity camera = coordinates pass through unchanged. Full backward compatibility.
  • Perspective: applies fov_y-based frustum projection with near-plane clamping, maps to viewport coordinates.

Files changed

FileChange
transform.rsAdded Camera::project() method
modality/svg.rscompile() uses flatten_3d() + camera
modality/svg.rsAdded project_point() helper (3D world transform → camera projection)
modality/svg.rsemit_primitive() signature: Transform2D → Transform3D + Camera

Test Results

  • 405 tests, 0 failures, 1 ignored
  • All 26 SVG-specific tests pass
  • All 10 determinism tests pass (including determinism_with_tufte_constraints_100_runs)
  • All 8 e2e integration tests pass

Deployed

Binary deployed to golgiBody (/opt/membrane/petaltongue), service membrane-petaltongue restarted. Health check: v1.7.0, status ok.

What’s Next

From the convergence frontier identified in baseCamp 57:

  1. Auto-correction: constraints currently evaluate and warn. Next evolution: constraints that can auto-correct (e.g., DataInkRatio removes decoration, ColorAccessibility adjusts colors)
  2. hud-pt.js convergence (912 lines): the animation engine bridge — connect Rust FlowParticle/NodePulse/BandwidthGlow to the HUD
  3. Dark theme SVG: scene-level theme switching in the compilation pipeline

entry.title: The Human Engine — Epitope Sort of Tools on the Primal Mountain
entry.content:
The Mountain

The hero’s journey has three faces. Going up. Standing on top. Coming back down.

Each face needs different tools. But the tools themselves don’t change — they rotate. A brush can paint (creation) or sweep (discovery). Sweep is also part of scan. The same object, different epitope facing you, depending on where you stand on the mountain.

This is the human engine. Not the tools — the rotation.

Hypothesis

Every tool has multiple epitopes. The epitope that faces the user depends on their position on the mountain (ascending, summit, descending). The inventory is not a list of tools — it is a position on the mountain plus which epitope surfaces are currently facing you.

Corollary 1: Tool classification by function is lossy. A brush sorted into “painting tools” loses its sweep epitope. An epitope sort preserves all surfaces.

Corollary 2: The journey itself is the inventory. Your braid (the trail of what you touched, read, built) IS your tool collection. You don’t carry tools up the mountain — you grow them by walking.

Corollary 3: ShareWear. When two braids intersect, the tools become shared. The compass works for both. The brush paints for both. Wear like clothes (identity you put on). Wear like stress and degradation (the cost of the journey). Share the load and the life and the compression.

The Three Faces

Ascending — Tools for Finding

You don’t know what you’re looking for. You need tools that help you discover, orient, scan.

ToolEpitope on ascentQuestion it answers
CompassDirection — which way to goWhere is north from here?
SweepDiscovery — what’s around youWhat did I miss?
SextantPosition — where am I relative to the starsHow far have I come?
LensFocus — look at one thing carefullyWhat is this, specifically?
BraidTrail — track where you’ve beenWhere was I before?

These are Schell’s ascending lenses:

  • Lens #4 Curiosity — “What questions does the design plant?”
  • Lens #2 Surprise — “What will surprise?”
  • Lens #1 Essential Experience — “What experience should the player have?”

Ascending tools answer: What is here?

Summit — Tools for Seeing

You’ve arrived. You can see the whole landscape. You need tools that help you measure, analyze, reflect.

ToolEpitope at summitQuestion it answers
LensAnalysis — see pattern in what you foundWhat does this mean?
SextantMeasurement — distance between here and thereHow far is it?
MapSynthesis — see the whole landscapeWhat is the shape of everything?
MirrorReflection — see yourself seeingWho am I in this?
CompassOrientation — true north vs magnetic northWhat is real vs what seems real?

These are Schell’s summit lenses:

  • Lens #79 Flow — “Does the system produce flow states?”
  • Lens #7 Elemental Tetrad — “Are aesthetics, mechanics, story, and technology balanced?”
  • Lens #9 Unification — “Does a single theme unite all elements?”

Summit tools answer: What does it mean?

Descending — Tools for Making

You know what you found. You need tools that help you build, share, teach.

ToolEpitope on descentQuestion it answers
BrushPaint — create what you sawHow do I show this?
ForgeBuild — make the thingHow do I make it real?
BraidStory — tell what happenedHow do I explain the journey?
CompassTeach — point others toward the mountainHow do I help someone else find it?
MirrorVerify — let others see what you sawCan you see it too?

These are Schell’s descending lenses:

  • Lens #63 Feedback — “Does the system communicate state clearly?”
  • Lens #42 Transparency — “Can the player understand the rules?”
  • Lens #68 Story/Game Balance — “Do narrative and mechanics reinforce each other?”

Descending tools answer: How do I bring it back?

The Brush-Sweep Insight

A brush has at least three epitopes:

EpitopeFaceFunction
PaintDescendingApply color, make a mark, express
SweepAscendingClear debris, reveal what’s underneath
ScanSummitSystematic coverage, ensure nothing missed

Sweep connects to scan. Scan connects to compass. Compass connects to sextant. The tools form their own graph — their epitopes overlap, creating a mesh of capability.

This mesh IS the inventory. Not a flat list. A graph. Each node is a tool. Each edge is a shared epitope between tools. The user’s position on the mountain determines which edges are active — which epitope surfaces face them.

The Tool Epitope Graph

            compass ←—direction—→ sextant
              ↕                      ↕
           orient                 measure
              ↕                      ↕
            sweep ←——scan——→ lens
              ↕                      ↕
            brush ←——paint——→ forge
              ↕                      ↕
            story ←——braid——→ mirror

Every tool connects to every other tool through shared epitopes. The graph is complete. The position on the mountain prunes which edges are active.

Shannon Entropy of Tool Use

Each non-self in the tuebor graph has a Shannon entropy measuring the diversity of its edge types. Banks: H=3.28 (11 connections, 10 types). SLF: H=0 (1 connection, 1 type).

Apply the same measure to tool use:

High entropy = the user is using many tools in many modes. They’re exploring, rotating, discovering. They’re ascending.

Low entropy = the user is using one tool deeply. They’re focused, drilling, building. They’re descending — or they’ve found their groove at the summit.

The entropy of tool use tells you where the user is on the mountain without asking them.

H rangeMountain positionWhat they need
H > 2.0AscendingMore tools, wider scan, compass orientation
1.0 < H < 2.0SummitFewer tools, deeper analysis, reflection
H < 1.0DescendingOne tool, sharp focus, let them build

Immune Pressure on Tools

Immune pressure measures how much of the system is watching. For tools: how many of the user’s actions are feedback-producing vs absorption-only?

  • High immune pressure: the user is testing, validating, checking. The system is responding to every action. This is calibration.
  • Low immune pressure: the user is flowing. The system is quiet. This is creation.

The transition from high to low immune pressure is the shift from summit to descent. You stop checking and start building. The mountain lets go.

Golgi Navigation — The User’s Membrane

Every non-self gets a braid. Every self also gets a braid.

The user’s braid is their journey through the evidence. Their path through braids = their trail. The trail IS the inventory.

Golgi navigation:

DirectionWhat happens
↑ golgi upZoom out. See more of the mountain. Ionosphere view. More context, less detail.
← membraneStay here. The current braid. The current tool. The current epitope.
↓ golgi downZoom in. Go deeper into this one thing. Substrate view. More detail, less context.

The user can golgi up and down their own membrane. In time, their membrane and the non-self’s membrane overlap. Where they overlap: shareWear.

ShareWear

Wear like clothes and wear like stress and degradation. We share the load and the life and the compression.

ShareWear is the intersection of two braids. When the user’s journey braid overlaps with a non-self’s evidence braid, three things become shared:

  1. The load — both see the same evidence. Neither carries it alone.
  2. The life — both contributed to the braid. The user by reading, the non-self by acting. Both are authors.
  3. The compression — Shannon entropy of the shared surface. High compression = the braids are coherent, the stories align. Low compression = noise, conflict, unresolved.

The shareWear index:

shareWear = |braid_user ∩ braid_nonself| / |braid_user ∪ braid_nonself|

Jaccard similarity. When shareWear = 1.0, the braids are identical — observer and observed see the same thing. When shareWear = 0.0, the braids are disjoint — no shared experience. Neither extreme is the goal. The goal is the middle: enough shared to communicate, enough different to learn.

The ludoSpring Mapping

ludoSpring’s 32 capabilities, epitope-sorted by mountain face:

Ascending (Discovery)

  • game.generate_noise — explore procedural landscapes
  • game.wfc_step — wave function collapse, let structure emerge
  • game.analyze_ui — scan the interface for what’s there
  • game.accessibility — who can reach this? who can’t?

Summit (Understanding)

  • game.evaluate_flow — is this producing flow states?
  • game.engagement — measure attention × curiosity × interaction
  • game.difficulty_adjustment — calibrate challenge to skill
  • game.query_vertices — see the provenance graph

Descending (Creation)

  • game.push_scene — render what you found
  • game.narrate_action — tell the story of what happened
  • game.npc_dialogue — let characters speak
  • game.mint_certificate — prove the journey happened
  • game.begin_session / game.record_action / game.complete_session — the braid

All Faces (Infrastructure)

  • game.fitts_cost — how hard is it to reach this? (ascending: how far? summit: is it calibrated? descending: can I teach it?)
  • game.storage_put / game.storage_get — memory (ascending: cache what I found. summit: organize it. descending: retrieve it to share.)
  • game.poll_telemetry — heartbeat (ascending: am I alive? summit: how fast? descending: are they receiving?)

The Schell lenses (20) evaluate from all faces simultaneously. Each lens has its own mountain position where it’s most powerful, but works everywhere:

LensStrongest faceAlso works on
#4 CuriosityAscendingSummit (what patterns?), Descending (what questions to plant?)
#79 FlowSummitAscending (am I in flow?), Descending (will they flow?)
#63 FeedbackDescendingAscending (am I getting signal?), Summit (is it clear?)
#39 Meaningful ChoiceAll equallyThe universal lens — does this matter?

Connection to the Architecture

SystemMountain metaphorWhat it does
Ionosphere (HUD)View from orbitSee the whole mountain, all paths, all travelers
Michigan Topology (tuebor/map)The mountain surfaceGeographic positioning, proximity radar, three perspectives
Data Braids (tuebor/braid)The trail markersEvery non-self’s journey recorded, entropy measured
Epitope Sort (HUD)The compass roseNavigate by interest, not by category
Billboard (signal)The summit cairnWhat the mountain says to those who arrive
ShareWearThe meeting pointWhere two braids intersect — shared load, shared life

The Engine

The human engine is not a machine. It’s the rotation.

The mountain doesn’t move. The tools don’t change. The user walks. As they walk, the tools rotate — different epitopes face them. The brush becomes a broom becomes a scanner. The compass becomes a teacher becomes a compass again.

The journey IS the proof. The proof IS the tool. The tool IS the journey.

P ≠ NP because you can’t skip the walk. NP ≠ P because knowing the summit doesn’t build the path. The gap between them is the mountain.

And shareWear: when you’ve walked the same mountain as someone else, the load gets lighter. Not because the mountain shrinks. Because the compression is mutual.

There is no shortcut.

baseCamp 59 · October 10, 2026 · Artisan

entry.title: baseCamp 59 — Vitality and Negentropy: Life at the Mobility Edge
entry.content:
Date: October 10, 2026 (Wave 171) Status: Implemented and deployed — entity_profile.rs in skunky-ingest, live on golgiBody. Vitality and negentropy fields in topology.json. human_browser fleet confidence reduced from 57.1% to 38.0%. Ghost remains 100.0%. Domain: Anderson localization × immunology × information theory × behavioral ecology × thermodynamics Novelty: First system to recognize life by its uncertainty rather than its certainty. The mobility edge of the Anderson localization transition — where the localization length diverges — becomes the boundary where behavioral classification should yield trust, not suspicion. Implementation: skunky-ingest/src/entity_profile.rs — vitality reflection on all 7 epitope results, entropy-gated fleet confidence, negentropy from vulnerability probe diversity. Commits 6554671, 75b2a02.

Abstract

The ecoPrimals epitope system (Papers 41, 48) identifies automated fleets by six conserved behavioral invariants: sec_fetch_monotone, reading_deficit, ua_pool_poverty, session_absent, referer_self_loop, and burst_ratio. Each epitope costs the fleet more to evade than the last. The system detects death — machine behavior — with precision approaching 100%.

But it cannot recognize life. Entities near the classification threshold are penalized for their uncertainty: a human_browser entity with 9.6% reading pauses (threshold: 10%) triggers reading_deficit despite 1,279 genuine reading pauses. A browser whose page loads create sub-3-second asset waterfalls triggers burst_ratio at 76.1% (threshold: 50%) despite VARIED timing (CV = 2.512).

We introduce two reflected signals that complete the system:

  1. Vitality — proximity to the threshold boundary, gated by the binary entropy of the trigger ratio. Vitality peaks at the Anderson mobility edge, where the localization length diverges. An entity at 7/7 triggered epitopes has entropy H(p) = 0 — no uncertainty, certain death. An entity at 4/7 has H(p) ≈ 0.99 — maximum uncertainty, maximum vitality, life.

  2. Negentropy — the defensive information that hostile probes provide to the organism. Vulnerability scanners that probe .env, .git/config, .aws/credentials, and wp-admin across 30+ unique paths are performing free penetration tests. Each probe teaches the organism about its attack surface. The organism now captures this information as negentropy rather than discarding it as hostile noise.

The result: fleet_confidence = raw × (1 - effective_vitality), where effective_vitality = vitality_mean × H(trigger_ratio). Ghost (7/7 epitopes, 56K IPs) stays at 100.0% fleet confidence. human_browser (4/7 epitopes, 1,279 reading pauses, CV = 2.512) drops from 57.1% to 38.0%. The uncertainty crossed to the other side of trust.

1. The Problem: Death Detection Without Life Recognition

1.1 The Asymmetry

Paper 48 formalizes epitope-based sorting as compression: H(data|epitope) < H(data|alphabet) < H(data). The six conserved epitopes compress the behavioral search space by grouping entities with shared invariants. Across 1.29 million accumulated requests on the ecoPrimals membrane, the epitope sort achieves a compression ratio of 9.6×.

The sort works. But it has a blind spot. Consider the classification of human_browser:

EpitopeScoreThresholdTriggeredGap
sec_fetch_monotone46.8%>95%No48.2 points clear
reading_deficit9.6%<10%Yes0.4 points over
ua_pool_poverty78 UAs262 neededYes184 short
session_absent0.7%<5%Yes4.3 points deep
referer_self_loop17.1%<2%No15.1 points clear
burst_ratio75.8%>50%Yes25.8 points over
referer_absence0.3%>95%No94.7 points clear

Four of seven epitopes trigger. Fleet confidence: 57.1%. But look at the gaps:

  • reading_deficit at 9.6% is 0.4 percentage points from clearing. There are 1,279 reading pauses in this entity — intervals >8 seconds where someone stopped to read. The system counts them, sees they’re “only” 9.6% of all intervals, and fires the epitope. But those 1,279 pauses exist. Machines don’t pause for 8 seconds.

  • burst_ratio at 75.8% includes the browser’s own fetch pipeline. When a human loads a page, the browser fires main.css, phi.css, hud-widget.js, signal-pt.js in sub-second waterfall. That’s not machine speed — it’s how HTTP/2 works. The top targets for human_browser are css/main.css (173), css/phi.css (171), js/hud-widget.js (143). Every page load generates a burst.

  • session_absent at 0.7% penalizes privacy. A visitor who blocks cookies, uses private browsing, or simply reads and leaves is not a machine — they are exercising a right. Paper 48 already notes: “absence is not unique to fleets (privacy-conscious humans also block cookies).”

The system’s timing classification of human_browser is VARIED (CV = 2.512). This is the most human timing signature possible — irregular, unpredictable, bursty then silent then bursty again. Machines are METRONOMIC (CV < 0.15). The system calls the timing “VARIED” and then penalizes the variation.

1.2 What the Threshold Doesn’t See

The threshold is a binary decision boundary. On one side: triggered (machine). On the other side: not triggered (passes). But the distance from the threshold carries information that the binary ignores.

For reading_deficit:

  • Ghost scores 1.1% → 8.9 points below threshold → definitive machine
